Scaling the Global Hausbank Deutsche Bank’s strategy, Scaling the Global Hausbank, focuses on accelerating value creation through focused growth, disciplined capital management and a scalable operating model. Shareholder value add (SVA) remains the central steering principle, guiding resource allocation and accountability across the bank. Key performance indicators for 2028: Financial targets: – Post-tax return on average tangible equity of greater than 13% for the Group – Cost/income ratio of below 60% Capital objectives: – CET1 capital ratio within an operating range of 13.5% to 14.0%, with a 200 basis points distance to the Maximum Distributable Amount (MDA) as a floor – 60% total payout ratio from 2026 and distribution of excess capital when CET1 capital ratio is sustainably above 14% Post-tax return on average tangible equity is a non-GAAP financial measure. Details on the definitions of such measures and reconciliations to the IFRS numbers on which they are based are available in the section “Non-GAAP financial measures” of this report. Deutsche Bank’s financial targets and capital objectives are based on the bank’s financial results prepared in accordance with the International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS) as issued by the International Accounting Standards Board (IASB) and endorsed by the European Union (EU). Further details are available in the section ‘Basis of preparation/impact of changes in accounting principles’ in this report. Progress on strategy implementation During the first nine months of 2026, Deutsche Bank made tangible progress in executing the bank’s strategy, with investments driving growth and improving efficiency across the franchise. Deutsche Bank continued to deliver revenue growth and remained on track to meet its full-year 2026 revenue ambition of around € 33 billion. Revenue growth was also in line with the bank’s planned growth trajectory through 2028. Focused growth areas contributed nearly 80% of the increase. The bank maintained a strong focus on strict capital discipline and continued to execute capital initiatives, including further capital-accretive actions on nonperforming exposures and progress on its securitization programs. The bank completed share buybacks totalling € 1.5 billion in 2026 (2025: € 1.0 billion). In addition, the bank made further progress on its scalable operating model by continuing to simplify the bank’s processes and made targeted investments in technology, as well as enhancing front-to-back capabilities across the Group. 4 Deutsche Bank Strategy Earnings Report as of September 30, 2026 Sustainability Deutsche Bank sustainability highlights included: – Jointly coordinating a € 1 billion syndicated guarantee facility for ENERCON to support the company’s continued development following its successful restructuring. The facility supports the production, distribution and servicing of onshore wind turbines. Deutsche Bank acted as bookrunner – Providing the Republic of Benin’s Ministry of Economy and Finance with a € 375 million loan facility under Benin’s Sustainable Development Goals Bond Framework. Proceeds intend to finance eligible expenditures including renewable energy and water access. Other priority investments include education, health, infrastructure, agriculture, and job creation for young people and women. Deutsche Bank acted as co-mandated lead arranger – Supporting TenneT Germany, a key enabler of the German energy transition, by contributing to a € 2.6 billion European Green Bond (EuGB) issuance, the largest corporate EuGB hybrid transaction to date. Proceeds will be allocated to eligible transmission infrastructure, enabling security of supply and renewable energy integration. Deutsche Bank acted as joint active bookrunner – Deutsche Bank updated its Transition Plan in September 2026, incorporating revised emissions data and reporting on progress towards its targets 5 Deutsche Bank Group results Earnings Report as of September 30, 2026 Group results The information presented in this section is based on IFRS as issued by the IASB (IASB IFRS), whereas Deutsche Bank’s financial targets and capital objectives are based on financial results prepared in accordance with IFRS as issued by the IASB and endorsed by the EU (EU IFRS). All rights reserved. 30 September 2026 Pillar 3 Report | UBS Group | Introduction and basis for preparation 2 UBS Group Introduction and basis for preparation Scope of Basel III Pillar 3 disclosures The Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (the BCBS) final Basel III capital adequacy framework consists of three complementary pillars. Pillar 1 provides a framework for measuring minimum capital requirements for the credit, market and operational risks faced by banks. Pillar 2 addresses the principles of the supervisory review process, emphasizing the need for a qualitative approach to supervising banks. Pillar 3 requires banks to publish a range of disclosures, mainly covering risk, capital, leverage, liquidity and remuneration. This report provides Pillar 3 disclosures for the UBS Group and prudential key figures and regulatory information for UBS AG consolidated and standalone, UBS Switzerland AG standalone, UBS Europe SE consolidated and UBS Americas Holding LLC consolidated in the respective sections under “Significant regulated subsidiaries and sub-groups”. This Pillar 3 report has been prepared in accordance with the Swiss Financial Market Supervisory Authority (FINMA) Ordinance on the Disclosure Obligations of Banks and Securities Firms (the DisO-FINMA), the corresponding explanatory notes, and the underlying BCBS Basel framework disclosure requirements. The revised Capital Adequacy Ordinance (the CAO) that incorporates the final Basel III standards into Swiss law, and the five new FINMA ordinances (including the DisO-FINMA) that contain the implementing provisions for the revised CAO, entered into force on 1 January 2025. The DisO-FINMA replaces FINMA Circular 2016/1 “Disclosure – banks” and incorporates in particular new and revised disclosure tables on risks and capital requirements. › Refer to “Changes to Pillar 3 disclosure requirements” in the “Introduction and basis for preparation” section of the 31 March 2025 Pillar 3 Report, available under “Pillar 3 disclosures” at ubs.com/investors , for information about new and revised quarterly tables as a result of the implementation of the final Basel III standards in Switzerland As UBS is a systemically relevant bank (an SRB) under Swiss banking law, UBS Group AG and UBS AG are required to comply with regulations based on the final Basel III framework as applicable to Swiss SRBs on a consolidated basis, whereas UBS Switzerland AG is exempt from consolidation. Local regulators may also require the publication of Pillar 3 information at a subsidiary or sub-group level. Where applicable, these local disclosures are provided under “Holding company and significant regulated subsidiaries and sub- groups” at ubs.com/investors . Significant regulatory developments, disclosure requirements and other changes Banking regulation in Switzerland In August 2026, the Swiss Federal Council launched two public consultations on further measures under the too-big-to- fail reform package, with one consultation covering proposed legislative measures and the other covering proposed amendments to the Swiss Liquidity Ordinance. The proposed legislative measures, to be submitted to the Swiss Parliament for enactment, include additional requirements for the recovery and resolution of systemically important banks (SIBs), add measures to enhance banks’ ability to obtain liquidity from the Swiss National Bank, introduce a Senior Managers Regime for banks with more complex organizational structures, and provide expanded supervisory powers for FINMA. This consultation will conclude in November 2026, and the Swiss Federal Council is expected to submit its final legislative proposal to the Swiss Parliament in the first half of 2027. The entry into force of these changes is expected no earlier than the beginning of 2029. The proposed amendments to the Swiss Liquidity Ordinance, including quantitative minimum requirements for borrowing capacity for emergency liquidity assistance, are subject to public consultation until November 2026. Related amendments are expected to enter into force no earlier than the beginning of 2029, with an expected phase in over a period of four years. In September 2026, the Council of States (the upper house of the Swiss Parliament) supported a proposal requiring SIBs to deduct 90% of the carrying value of foreign participations from regulatory capital, with the deduction to be made entirely from common equity tier 1 (CET1) capital. This proposal is now subject to the deliberations of the National Council (the lower house of the Swiss Parliament). If enacted in the form supported by the Council of States, the proposal is expected to be phased in commencing in 2028, at the earliest, and would require UBS AG to hold approximately USD 16bn of additional CET1 capital. This would come in addition to around USD 2bn of additional CET1 capital required at UBS AG as a result of the ordinance-level measures announced earlier this year. UBS AG must also hold the previously disclosed CET1 capital of around USD 15bn under existing regulations following the acquisition of Credit Suisse. This amount includes around USD 9bn related to regulatory concessions granted to Credit Suisse and around USD 6bn to meet the current progressive requirements due to the increased size and market share of the combined business. 30 September 2026 Pillar 3 Report | UBS Group | Introduction and basis for preparation 3 If the decision by the Council of States is confirmed, UBS would be required to hold a total of around USD 33bn of incremental CET1 capital since the acquisition of Credit Suisse. In parallel, once implemented, the ordinance-level changes announced earlier this year would eliminate an estimated USD 4bn of CET1 capital at the Group level. The total annual capital-related cost resulting from the acquisition would amount to around USD 2.5bn. Other developments Capital returns In the third quarter of 2026 we repurchased USD 1,807m of shares under our 2026 share repurchase programs. We expect to complete our current USD 3bn share repurchase program by the time of the publication of our fourth-quarter 2026 results. The amount and pace of share repurchases will remain subject to our short-term financial performance and outlook, maintaining a CET1 capital ratio of around 14% and further visibility on the deliberations by the Swiss Parliament on the capitalization of foreign subsidiaries. The KM2 table includes a reference to the total loss-absorbing capacity (TLAC) term sheet, published by the Financial Stability Board (the FSB). The FSB provides this term sheet at fsb.org/2015/11/total-loss-absorbing-capacity-tlac-principles-and-term-sheet . Our tier 1 capital ratio increased, reflecting a decrease in risk-weighted assets (RWA), partly offset by a decrease in our tier 1 capital. Our Basel III leverage ratio increased, driven by a decrease in the leverage ratio denominator (the LRD), partly offset by a decrease in our tier 1 capital. Our common equity tier 1 (CET1) capital increased by USD 0.7bn to USD 73.1bn, mainly reflecting operating profit before tax of USD 3.6bn, partly offset by dividend accruals of USD 0.9bn, negative foreign currency translation effects of USD 0.7bn, a USD 0.7bn negative effect from compensation- and own-share-related components, and current tax expenses of USD 0.6bn. Share repurchases of USD 1.8bn made under our 2026 share repurchase programs in the third quarter of 2026 did not affect our CET1 capital position, as there was an identical reduction in the existing capital reserve for expected future share repurchases. Our tier 1 capital decreased by USD 0.1bn to USD 95.9bn, reflecting the aforementioned USD 0.7bn increase in CET1 capital, which was more than offset by a USD 0.7bn decrease in additional tier 1 (AT1) capital. The decrease in AT1 capital reflected negative impacts from interest rate risk hedge, foreign currency translation and other effects. The TLAC available as of 30 September 2026 included CET1 capital, AT1 capital and non-regulatory capital elements of TLAC. Our available TLAC decreased by USD 6.9bn to USD 186.7bn, reflecting the aforementioned decrease in tier 1 capital and a USD 6.9bn decrease in non-regulatory capital elements of TLAC. The decrease in non-regulatory elements of TLAC was mainly driven by USD 9.7bn of TLAC-eligible senior unsecured debt instruments (USD 9.8bn in notional amount) that we repurchased in September 2026, the redemption of TLAC-eligible senior unsecured debt instruments for the equivalent of USD 4.7bn and negative impacts from interest rate risk hedge, foreign currency translation and other effects. These decreases were partly offset by new issuances of TLAC-eligible senior unsecured debt instruments totaling the equivalent of USD 11.1bn. During the third quarter of 2026, RWA decreased by USD 7.8bn to USD 496.1bn, driven by a USD 4.7bn decrease from currency effects, a USD 2.8bn decrease resulting from asset size and other movements, and a USD 0.2bn decrease driven by model updates and methodology changes. During the third quarter of 2026, the LRD decreased by USD 58.6bn to USD 1,591.2bn, driven by a USD 38.3bn decrease from asset size and other movements and a USD 20.3bn decrease from currency effects. The quarterly average liquidity coverage ratio of the UBS Group increased 1.4 percentage points to 178.7%, remaining above the prudential requirement communicated by FINMA. Average net cash outflows decreased by USD 11.4bn to USD 181.5bn, primarily reflecting lower outflows from customer deposits and higher net inflows from securities financing transactions, partly offset by lower inflows from lending assets. The effect of the decrease in net cash outflows was partly offset by a USD 17.5bn decrease in average high-quality liquid assets to USD 324.3bn, mainly reflecting lower cash available from decreases in customer deposits, primarily from currency effects, and in debt issued at amortized cost, partly offset by higher cash available from lower lending assets. As of 30 September 2026, the net stable funding ratio of the UBS Group decreased 0.3 percentage points to 114.8%, remaining above the prudential requirement communicated by FINMA. Available stable funding decreased by USD 11.5bn to USD 888.8bn, mainly driven by lower debt issued at amortized cost. text: EX-99.1 2 exh_991.htm PRESS RELEASE EdgarFiling EXHIBIT 99.1 ING announces new distribution programme of up to €1.9 billion ING announces new distribution programme of up to €1.9 billion ING announced today a shareholder distribution of up to €1.9 billion. The distribution consists of a share buyback programme for a maximum total amount of €1.65 billion and a cash payment of €0.25 billion. The purpose of the distribution is to maintain our CET1 ratio in line with our target of ~13%. ING Group’s CET1 ratio was 13.3% at the end of the third quarter of 2026, which is well above the prevailing CET1 ratio requirement of 11.10%. In line with ING’s dividend reserving approach, the additional distribution will be financed from dividend reserves. As a result, the implied CET1 impact of 56 bps is already reflected in the reported 13.3% CET1 ratio for 3Q2026. The share buyback programme will commence on 29 October 2026 and is expected to end no later than 26 April 2027. The €0.25 billion in cash will be paid on 14 January 2027. The ECB has approved the distribution, and the share buyback programme will be executed in compliance with the Market Abuse Regulation and within the limitations of the existing authority to acquire a maximum of 20% of the issued shares as granted by the general meeting of shareholders on 14 April 2026. ING has entered a non-discretionary arrangement with a financial intermediary to conduct the buyback. We provide weekly updates on the progress of the programme via a press release and on the share buyback programme page on our website. Note for editors For further information on ING, please visit www.ing.com. Frequent news updates can be found in the Newsroom. Photos of ING operations, buildings and its executives are available for download at Flickr. Press enquiries Investor enquiries ING Group Media Relations ING Group Investor Relations +31 20 576 5000 +31 20 576 6396 Media.relations@ing.com Investor.Relations@ing.com ING PROFILE ING is a global financial institution with a strong European base, offering banking services through its operating company ING bank. The purpose of ING Bank is: empowering people to stay a step ahead in life and in business. ING Bank’s more than 60,000 employees offer retail and wholesale banking services to customers in over 100 countries. ING Group shares are listed on the exchanges of Amsterdam (INGA NA, INGA.AS), Brussels and on the New York Stock Exchange (ADRs: ING US, ING.N). ING aims to put sustainability at the heart of what we do. Our policies and actions are assessed by independent research and ratings providers, which give updates on them annually. ING's ESG rating by MSCI has been upgraded from 'AA' to 'AAA' in October 2025. As of July 2026, in Sustainalytics’ view, ING’s management of ESG material risk is ‘Strong’ with an ESG risk rating of 16.7 (low risk). ING Group shares are also included in major sustainability and ESG index products of leading providers. Here are some examples: Euronext, STOXX, Morningstar and FTSE Russell. HSBC Holdings plc Earnings Release 3Q26 on Form 6-K 1 H SBC H oldi ngs p lc Earnings Release 3Q26 27 October 2026 Georges Elhedery, Group CEO, said: “Our performance shows that in a more complex world clients continue to turn to us to navigate uncertainty and seize new opportunities. It also reflects consistent execution of our strategic priorities with pace, precision and discipline. As we simplify HSBC, we are creating greater capacity to invest, grow and deliver strong returns for our shareholders.” Financial performance in 3Q26 – Profit before tax increased by $2.3bn or 32% to $9.6bn compared with 3Q25, primarily due to a net favourable impact from notable items of $1.4bn , which reflected the non-recurrence of legal provisions in 3Q25 of $1.4bn . The increase also reflected growth in revenue, mainly from banking net interest income (‘banking NII’) and lower expected credit losses and other credit impairment charges (‘ECL’). Profit after tax increased by $2.1bn or 38% to $7.6bn compared with 3Q25. – Constant currency profit before tax excluding notable items increased by $0.9bn to $10.0bn compared with 3Q25. – Annualised return on average tangible equity (‘RoTE‘) in 3Q26 was 17.7% compared with 12.3% in 3Q25. Excluding notable items, annualised RoTE in 3Q26 was 18.2% , a rise of 1.6 p ercentage points compared with 3Q25. – Revenue increased by $ 0.8 bn to $18.6bn compared with 3Q25, primarily reflecting growth in banking NII. F ee and other income also increased in our Corporate and Institutional Banking (‘CIB’) business in Wholesale Transaction Banking (‘WTB’) and in Debt and Equity Markets , supported by higher customer activity, and in Investment Distribution and Private Bank in Wealth. This was partly offset by valuation losses in Corporate Centre and t he non-recurrence of one-off favourable impacts in 3Q25 in Insurance . Constant currency revenue excluding notable items rose by $0.8bn to $18.7bn . – Net interest income (‘NII’) of $9.3bn increased by $0.5bn or 6% compared with 3Q25. The increase reflected deposit balance growth and the benefit of reinvestment of our structural hedge at higher yields, partly offset by lower NII from Markets Treasury and an adverse impact of $0.1bn from one-off items in 3Q26. Banking NII increased by $0.6bn to $11.7bn . Banking NII excludes insurance NII, which fell by $0.1bn, and the funding costs associated with the trading book, which remained broadly stable. – Net interest margin (‘NIM’) of 1.57% was stable compared with 3Q25. – ECL of $0.8bn decreased by $0.2bn or 17% compared with 3Q25, primarily reflecting a $0.1bn reduction in stage 3 charges related to the Hong Kong commercial real estate (‘CRE’) sector, as well as l ower charges in our UK business and International Wealth and Premier Banking (‘IWPB’) b usiness in Mexico. – Operating expenses of $8.8bn were $1.3bn or 12% lower compared with 3Q25. This included a favourable net impact of $1.4bn from notable items, which reflected the non-recurrence of legal provisions in 3Q25. Excluding notable items, the increase in operating expenses primarily reflected the impact of inflation, higher planned spend and investment in technology , and the phasing of the performance-related pay accrual relative to 3Q25, partly mitigated by the cost reduction benefits from our organisational simplification. Target basis operating expenses were $0.1bn or 1.4% higher than in 3Q25, including the impact of inflation and higher planned spend and investment in technology, partly offset by the cost reduction benefits from our organisational simplification. – Customer lending balances increased by $7.8bn compared with 2Q26 on a reported basis. On a constant currency basis, lending balances increased by $6.7bn . This primarily reflected growth as we supported our customers to participate in the India Foreign Currency Non-Resident Deposit scheme , together with growth in our U K and Hong Kong businesses. This was partly offset by the classification to held for sale of lending balances associated with the exit of our retail banking business in Australia in our IWPB business . – Customer accounts increased by $9.1bn compared with 2Q26 on a reported basis. On a constant currency basis, customer accounts increased by $6.5bn , reflecting continued momentum in deposit inflows in our Hong Kong business. In our IWPB business, deposit growth was mainly in India, as we facilitated customer participation i n the India Foreign Currency Non-Resident Deposit scheme. This growth was partly offset by retail deposit outflows following our announced exit of our retail banking business in Australia. In CIB, lower deposit balances reflected outflows of short-term balances . – Common equity tier 1 (‘CET1’) capital ratio of 13.9% decreased by 0.2 percentage points compared with 30 June 2026, reflecting an increase in risk-weighted assets (‘RWAs‘), together with a decrease in the fair value of hold-to-collect-and-sell debt instruments due to higher yields and the impact of the share buy-bac k announced at our interim results, partly offset by regulatory profits net of dividends. – The Board has approved a third interim dividend of $0.10 per share. On 28 September 2026, we completed the $1bn share buy-back announced at our i nterim results . We also intend to initiate a share buy-back of up to $1bn, which we expect to complete by our 2026 full- year results announcement. Financial performance in 9M26 – Profit before tax increased by $6.0bn or 26% to $29.2bn compared with 9M25. The increase primarily reflected a net favourable impact of $3.7bn from notable items. The increase also reflected revenue growth from an increase in banking NII and higher fee and other income, primarily in Wealth and WTB. Profit after tax of $22.9bn was $4.9bn or 28% higher compared with 9M25. – The net favourable movement in notable items primarily reflected the non-recurrence of 9M25 dilution and impairment losses of $2.1bn related to our associate Bank of Communications Co., Limited (‘BoCom’) and legal provisions of $1.4bn , together with lower restructuring costs associated with our organisational simplification of $0.3bn . These items were partly offset by disposal losses recognised on the classification to held for sale associated with the planned sale of our business in Malta of $0.3 bn in 9M26. – Constant currency profit before tax excluding notable items increased by $2.0bn to $30.4bn compared with 9M25. – Annualised RoTE in 9M26 was 18.0% . Excluding notable items, annualised RoTE in 9M26 was 18.8% , a rise of 1.1 percentage points compared with 9M 25 . HSBC Holdings plc Earnings Release 3Q26 on Form 6-K 2 – Revenue increased by $4.5bn or 9% to $56.4bn compared with 9M25, including a net favourable impact from notable items of $0.9bn and a favourable impact from foreign currency translation differences of $0.7bn . The remaining increase reflected higher banking NII, and fee and other income growth in Wealth across our IWPB and Hong Kong businesses, supported by higher customer activity, and in WTB, mainly in our CIB business. Constant currency revenue excluding notable items rose by $2.8bn to $56.8bn compared with 9M25. – NII increased by $1.9bn compared with 9M25, primarily driven by deposit balance growth, the benefit of reinvestment of our structural hedge at higher yields, and the favourable impact of foreign currency translation differences of $0.4bn . This was partly offset by lower NII from Markets Treasury. Banking NII increased by $2.2bn to $34.6bn , as the deduction for insurance NII reduced by $0.2bn, due to the impact of strategic transactions. The funding costs associated with the trading book, which are also excluded from banking NII, rose by $0.1bn. – NIM of 1.60% was 3 basis points (‘bps‘) higher compared with 9M25, mainly due to the impact from foreign currency translation differences and the benefit of our structural hedge, partly offset by lower market interest rates. – ECL of $3.2bn were $0.2bn higher than in 9M25. The 9M26 charge primarily reflected stage 3 charges on wholesale exposures, including a $0.5bn fraud-related, secondary , securitisation exposure with a financial sponsor in the UK in our CIB business. The 9M26 charge also included $0.3bn related to the Hong Kong CRE sector and allowances to reflect uncertainty due to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. ECL in 9M25 included charges of $0.7bn related to the Hong Kong CRE sector and a charge against a Middle Eastern exposure . – Operating expenses of $26.2bn were $0.9bn or 3% lower than in 9M25, including a favourable net impact of $1.8bn from notable items, which comprised the non-recurrence of legal provisions in 9M25 of $1.4bn and lower restructuring and other related costs associated with our organisational simplification of $0.3bn . Excluding notable items, the increase in expenses primarily reflected an adverse impact of $0.4bn from foreign currency translation differences, higher planned spend and investment in technology and Wealth, and the impact of inflation, partly mitigated by cost reductions from our organisational simplification. Target basis operating expenses were $0.5bn or 2.0% higher than in 9M25, including higher planned spend and investment in technology and the impact of inflation, partly offset by cost reductions from our organisational simplification. Outlook Group financial targets – We remain confident in achieving the targets we set out in February 2026, including a RoTE of 17% or better for 2026, 2027 and 2028, excluding notable items. – We continue to target year-on-year growth in revenue from 2026 to 2028, rising to 5% growth in 2028 compared with 2027, excluding notable items and on a constant currency basis. – We maintain our dividend payout ratio target basis of 50% for 2026, 2027 and 2028. Our target basis payout ratio is calculated as a percentage of earnings per share, excluding material notable items and related impacts. In respect of 2026 – We continue to expect banking NII of at least $46bn in 2026 . – We continue to expect an ECL charge as a percentage of average gross customer loans of around 45bps (including held for sale loan balances) for 2026. Over the medium term, we retain our planning range of 30–40bps. – The Group remains on track to deliver year-on-year growth in operating expenses of approximately 1% in 2026 on a target basis. As communicated at our 2026 interim results, should strong business performance continue, we may consider additional performance-related pay, which would increase 2026 target basis cost growth modestly. Our target basis operating expenses measure excludes notable items and includes the impact of simplification-related saves associated with our announced strategic reorganisation. Capital and regulatory developments – We continue to assess the anticipated impact of the final Basel 3.1 standards on our capital. We expect, based on our latest modelling, that the impact on the Group CET1 capital ratio a t 1 January 2027 will be a benefit of approximately 40–50bps. The final impact will depend on a number of factors, including model and data refinements, portfolio size and composition and supervisory permissions granted. Any related reductions to firm-specific capital requirements are not expected to be significant. – We intend to continue to manage our CET1 capital ratio within our medium-term target operating range of 14% to 14.5%.
